title: Security Review Positioning Notes (AEs/SEs) — Redwood Inference
author: Soojin Lee
body:
h1. Purpose
This page gives AEs and SEs a consistent way to position Redwood Inference during customer security reviews. It is designed to reduce back-and-forth, avoid over-committing, and make it clear how responsibilities change across *Hosted*, *Dedicated*, and *Private* deployments.

Use this alongside:
* *Enterprise Security FAQ v2* (canonical approved language)
* One-pagers (data residency, retention, audit logging, SSO/RBAC, incident response)
* Standard RFP Response Library (boilerplate + evidence pointers)

h1. Top-level messaging (what to lead with)
*Redwood is a developer-first inference platform built for production.* Our enterprise security posture is anchored in:
1) *Deployment flexibility with consistent controls* (Hosted, Dedicated, Private)
2) *Clear shared responsibility boundaries* and predictable operational posture
3) *Operational security fundamentals* (secure SDLC, vulnerability management, monitoring, incident response)
4) *Enterprise access controls and auditability* (SSO/RBAC + audit logs + evidence process)

h2. One-sentence positioning (use in emails)
“Redwood provides production-grade LLM inference with enterprise security controls and clear shared-responsibility boundaries across Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments—so teams can meet security requirements without rebuilding inference infrastructure.”

h2. What not to do
* Don’t invent commitments (e.g., “we always notify within X hours,” “logs are never stored,” “we are HIPAA compliant by default”).
* Don’t forward restricted artifacts (SOC 2 report, pen test details) outside the approved evidence flow.
* Don’t blur product boundaries: *Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private* differ materially in who operates what.

h1. Deployment modes: how to position and when to recommend
h2. Quick decision guide
* *Hosted API* — fastest onboarding; best for teams without strict isolation requirements.
* *Dedicated* — for predictable throughput and stronger isolation requirements (single-tenant compute pool; Redwood-operated).
* *Private (VPC / on-prem)* — for regulated workloads requiring customer-controlled networking and stronger boundary control; customer has more operational responsibility.

h2. Shared responsibility snapshot (talk track)
Use this framing:
*“Redwood provides the secure platform and operational controls for the components we operate, and customers retain responsibility for their application, data governance, identity governance, and how they use the model outputs. As you move from Hosted → Dedicated → Private, customer control increases, and so does customer operational responsibility.”*

h2. Shared responsibility matrix (high level)
|| Area || Hosted || Dedicated || Private (VPC / on-prem) ||
| *Model serving runtime + orchestration* | Redwood operated | Redwood operated | Customer operated (Redwood provides package/support per contract) |
| *Underlying infrastructure* | Redwood/Cloud provider | Redwood/Cloud provider (isolated pool) | Customer (VPC account / on-prem environment) |
| *Network boundary* | Redwood-managed | Redwood-managed (customer-specific isolation) | Customer-managed (VPC controls / on-prem network) |
| *Identity & access* | SSO/RBAC supported; customer config | Same | Same, plus customer-side IAM for infra |
| *Audit logging* | Redwood platform logs available | Same | Varies by architecture; customer retains infra logs; Redwood components produce logs per deployment design |
| *Data retention controls* | Redwood defaults + available configuration | Same | Customer-defined (plus Redwood component behavior per deployment) |
| *Key management options* | Redwood-managed keys; enterprise options via documented integrations where applicable | Same | Customer-managed keys typically expected; integration options depend on deployment |
| *Incident response* | Redwood incident process for Redwood-operated services | Same | Split: Redwood for supported components; customer for customer-operated infrastructure |

Note: For *exact wording* and the current product reality, use the Security FAQ v2 and the relevant one-pagers.

h1. Standard “how we run security” narrative (2–3 minutes)
Use this structure on calls:
1) *Security program & governance:* “We run a centralized security and compliance program and publish a consistent set of enterprise-facing artifacts and answers through our Security FAQ and RFP library.”
2) *Access controls & auditability:* “Enterprise customers commonly start by validating identity (SSO/SAML), role-based access control, and audit logging. Redwood supports these patterns and provides audit trails appropriate to the deployment mode.”
3) *Data handling controls:* “We clarify what data is processed, where it can be processed (residency), what gets logged, and retention options. Dedicated and Private change the data flow and isolation boundary.”
4) *Operational security:* “We have vulnerability management practices, secure development lifecycle controls, and an incident response process. Evidence is shared via our controlled process when needed.”

h1. Common customer objections + recommended responses
h2. “Are you SOC 2 certified? What’s in scope?”
*Positioning:*
* “We maintain a SOC 2 program and can share the report under NDA through our evidence process.”
* “Scope questions matter—tell us what systems you need covered (control plane, hosted inference services, support systems). We’ll map it to the report scope during the review.”

*Do:* Offer the one-pager (SOC 2 posture if included in the kit) and route report access via GRC.

*Don’t:* State “everything is covered” or share the report directly.

*Escalate to:* Olga Petrov / Daniel Carter for evidence access.

h2. “Do you train on our data? Do you use prompts for model training?”
*Positioning:*
* “Redwood’s inference platform processes customer inputs to generate outputs. We don’t position the product as a model training service.”
* “We can walk through how data flows and what is logged by default, and what retention controls are available by deployment mode.”

*Important:* Avoid absolute statements unless using approved FAQ language. Use the *data retention controls* one-pager for specifics.

h2. “Where is data stored? We require EU-only processing.”
*Positioning:*
* “Data residency depends on deployment mode and the region(s) you choose. We can support region-based processing and will confirm what telemetry/logs are generated and where they’re handled.”
* “For strict residency requirements, Dedicated or Private may be the right fit depending on your isolation and network constraints.”

*Artifacts:* Data Residency one-pager.

*Follow-up questions to ask:*
* “Is the requirement about *processing location*, *storage location*, or both?”
* “Does it apply to *application data*, *logs/telemetry*, and/or *support artifacts*?”

h2. “What do you log? Can we export audit logs to our SIEM?”
*Positioning:*
* “Redwood provides audit logging for administrative and platform events; what’s available depends on the deployment mode. We can share the categories of events, and export/integration options.”

*Artifacts:* Audit Logging Overview one-pager.

*Do:* Offer a sample event list *only* from the approved one-pager / RFP library.

*Don’t:* Promise roadmap items or event types not currently produced.

h2. “Do you support SSO/SAML? Do you support SCIM?”
*Positioning:*
* “We support enterprise authentication patterns (SSO/SAML) and role-based access control. Provisioning support (e.g., SCIM) is covered in the SSO/SAML/SCIM one-pager; we can confirm fit based on your IdP and desired lifecycle flows.”

*Artifacts:* SSO/SAML and SCIM one-pager + RBAC model reference (if deeper review requested).

h2. “We need customer-managed keys / HSM.”
*Positioning:*
* “Key management options vary by deployment model. Private deployments typically provide the most flexibility for customer-managed keys and customer-controlled crypto boundaries. For Hosted/Dedicated, we can explain current supported integrations and the boundary.”

*Do:* Keep this concrete and scoped to documented capabilities.

*Escalate to:* Security Eng (Marcus Lin) + Private SME (Colin O'Donnell) for architecture-specific questions.

h2. “We require a 24-hour breach notification clause.”
*Positioning:*
* “We have an incident response and customer notification process; exact notification timelines are contract-dependent and handled through Legal/Security.”
* “We can share our incident response and notification one-pager, and loop in the right owners for contractual language.”

*Artifacts:* Incident Response and Notification one-pager.

*Escalate to:* Legal (Michael Grant / Sofia Mendes) + GRC (Olga Petrov).

h2. “Your product uses sub-processors—who are they? Can we review DPAs?”
*Positioning:*
* “We maintain a subprocessor posture and can provide the current list through the approved channel. DPAs and legal terms are handled via our Legal team.”

*Do:* Share the customer-facing subprocessor list if/when it is part of the approved kit. Otherwise route to GRC.

h2. “We need on-prem / air-gapped.”
*Positioning:*
* “Private deployment options exist for regulated or constrained environments. The security boundary and operational responsibilities shift significantly—success depends on the desired connectivity, update cadence, logging/monitoring approach, and who operates day-to-day.”

*Qualify early:*
* “Is any outbound connectivity allowed (artifact fetch, updates, support)?”
* “Who will own patching and vulnerability remediation in the environment?”

*Escalate to:* Private deployments SME (Colin O'Donnell) + Security PM (Naomi Feldman).

h1. Proof points to emphasize (what customers care about)
Pick 3–5 based on the account:
* *Clarity of boundary:* We explicitly document what Redwood operates vs what the customer operates across Hosted/Dedicated/Private.
* *Auditability:* Administrative actions and key platform events are auditable; exports/integrations are available per documented options.
* *Enterprise identity:* SSO and RBAC enable least-privilege patterns.
* *Operational maturity:* Documented incident response and vulnerability management practices.
* *Pragmatic evidence flow:* We can move fast through questionnaires using a standardized RFP library and controlled evidence sharing.

h1. Deal mechanics: how to run a security review efficiently
h2. Recommended process (AE/SE checklist)
1) *Ask for their questionnaire upfront* (or their top 10 controls) and their required timeline.
2) Send the *field-ready PDF kit* (Security FAQ v2 + one-pagers) and offer to schedule a 30-minute security review call.
3) For evidence requests (SOC 2 report, pen test summaries), route through the *Customer Security Review Process* page (restricted) and involve GRC.
4) Keep a single source of truth in the deal record (e.g., link the Confluence canonical pages + the exact PDF version sent).
5) Track “open items” explicitly: residency, retention, audit log export, incident notification language, Private boundary.

h2. What to log in the deal notes (minimum)
* Deployment mode (Hosted/Dedicated/Private) + region(s)
* Customer’s hard requirements vs preferences
* Evidence requested (SOC 2 report, pen test summary, subprocessor list, DPA)
* Owner assigned (AE/SE/GRC/Legal/Security Eng)
* Date artifacts were sent and under what conditions (e.g., NDA)

h1. Approved language guardrails
Use these guardrails when speaking or writing:
* Prefer *“supports,” “available,” “configurable,” “contract-dependent,” “by deployment mode”*.
* Avoid absolutes like *“never,” “always,” “guaranteed,” “fully compliant”*.
* If you can’t find an answer in the FAQ v2 or RFP library, *don’t improvise*—route to Security/GRC.

h1. FAQs for AEs/SEs (internal)
h2. “Can I share the SOC 2 report directly?”
No. Follow the evidence sharing process and confirm NDA requirements. Route to GRC.

h2. “Customer wants a custom attestation letter.”
Route to GRC and Legal. Do not create ad-hoc letters.

h2. “Customer is asking about roadmap security features.”
You may discuss roadmap only at a high level and only if already approved for field use. Do not commit to dates or scope in writing.

h1. Quick email templates
h2. Sending the standard kit
Subject: Redwood security review materials

Hi <Name>,

Sharing Redwood’s current enterprise security review materials:
* Security FAQ v2 (deployment-mode specific)
* One-pagers: SSO/RBAC, audit logging, data residency, retention, incident response

If you share your questionnaire or top security requirements, we can respond using our standardized RFP library and pull any needed evidence via our controlled process.

Best,
<Name>

h2. Evidence request acknowledgment (SOC 2 / pen test)
Subject: Re: evidence request

Hi <Name>,

Thanks—SOC 2 and related evidence are available via our standard evidence-sharing process (typically under NDA, depending on the artifact). If you confirm your preferred NDA path, we can coordinate access and track distribution.

Best,
<Name>

h1. Escalation map (who to pull in)
* *GRC / evidence sharing / SOC 2 / subprocessors:* Olga Petrov, Daniel Carter
* *Security posture / product security questions:* Marcus Lin, Naomi Feldman
* *Audit logging + retention specifics:* Kevin Osei
* *Private deployment boundary / regulated environments:* Colin O'Donnell, Fatima Noor
* *Contract language (notification timelines, DPA, security appendix redlines):* Michael Grant, Sofia Mendes

h1. Change control
This page is a sales enablement artifact and must stay aligned with:
* Enterprise Security FAQ v2
* Standard RFP Response Library
* Customer-facing one-pagers

If you see field confusion or a recurring objection, add it to the quarterly review queue (tag Naomi Feldman + Markus Klein) and include:
* customer question verbatim
* why the current materials didn’t answer it
* suggested answer or needed SME

Footer: Version aligned with Security Enablement Kit v2. Last reviewed: 2026-02-21.
